modern_osis:
Verse 1 — The Lord governs every heart

As a farmer directs water through the land, God directs human hearts as he chooses. Believers therefore ask him to turn their own hearts and others' hearts toward faith, reverence and love.

Verse 2 — Do not trust self-assessment

We are partial and biased when judging our own motives and actions.

Verse 3 — Outward worship cannot excuse injustice

Many deceive themselves by imagining that religious ceremonies make unjust behavior acceptable.

Verse 4 — Sin becomes the wicked person's life

Pride, ambition, honor, joy and daily occupation can all become expressions of a wicked person's devotion to sin.

Verse 5 — Diligence plans ahead

Truly diligent people combine steady work with thoughtful preparation.

Verse 6 — Unlawful wealth brings death

Those seeking riches through forbidden practices are actually pursuing their own ruin.

Verse 7 — Injustice returns upon its author

The injuries people inflict through injustice eventually rebound upon them, bringing destruction both here and hereafter.

Verse 8 — The crookedness of fallen nature

Without divine grace, humanity's ways are perverse and estranged from God.

Verse 9 — Seek relief from quarrels through prayer

It is wiser to avoid bitter conflict by pouring our hearts out before God. Through prudence, patience and constant prayer, God may remove the burden.

Verse 10 — Evil desires corrupt conduct

The wicked heart's desires lead to degrading behavior.

Verse 11 — Learn from warning and teaching

The inexperienced can learn wisdom from the punishment of evildoers and from instruction given to willing students.

Verse 12 — Do not envy evil prosperity

Good people recognize the curse hidden in the apparent success of wicked people and do not envy them.

Verse 13 — Listen to the poor

Those who oppress poor workers through low wages, refuse help when able, or neglect justice while in authority stop their ears to the needy. Charity still requires wise discernment, but not hardness of heart.

Verse 14 — Restrain passions by better motives

If money can calm human fury, surely reason, reverence for God and Christ's command should be strong enough to restrain it.

Verse 15 — The joy of true faith

Genuine joy is found in living according to true religion.

Verse 16 — Even straying sinners may return

Those who turn deliberately toward spiritual darkness are in special danger. Yet the all-sufficient Savior still offers hope: let them flee to him without delay.

Verse 17 — Worldly pleasure brings ruin

A life dedicated to sinful and worldly pleasures leads to destruction.

Verse 18 — God's providence delivers the righteous

The righteous may be delivered from trouble while the wicked fall into it instead, appearing almost as a ransom in their place.

Verse 19 — Unrestrained passions ruin relationships

Unchecked passions destroy peace and comfort within families and other close relationships.

Verse 20 — Prudence preserves provision

Abundance gained through wisdom, steady work and thrift is valuable. Foolish people waste what they possess on selfish desires.

Verse 21 — Faith produces a righteous life

True repentance and trust in God's mercy through Jesus Christ lead believers to pursue righteousness and mercy in their own conduct.

Verse 22 — Wisdom may overcome strength

Wise people can accomplish great things even against opponents confident in their superior physical power.

Verse 23 — Keep the soul from needless trouble

We should especially guard our souls against becoming trapped, agitated and disturbed.

Verse 24 — Pride becomes habitual anger

Proud and arrogant people often become so passionate that anger seems to be their regular occupation.

Verses 25 and 26 — The misery of laziness and greed

The lazy person's hands refuse honest work that could supply a living, while the heart never stops craving wealth, pleasure and honor. The righteous and industrious find their legitimate desires satisfied.

Verse 27 — Hypocritical worship is hateful

It is especially detestable to pretend holiness while secretly intending wickedness.

Verse 28 — False witnesses face judgment

Those who bear false testimony cannot escape its ultimate consequences.

Verse 29 — Ask what God requires

Wicked people defy both God's law and Providence's warnings. Good people ask instead, “What does God require of me?”

Verses 30 and 31 — Means are necessary, but salvation comes from God

We must make responsible use of available means, but our safety and salvation belong to the Lord alone. In spiritual warfare, put on the whole armor of God, relying for strength upon his mighty power.

Verse 1 — Value a good reputation

We should be more careful to acquire and preserve a good name than to increase our wealth.

Verse 2 — Rich and poor before God

Providence has ordered that some people are wealthy and others poor. Yet all are sinners before God, and the poor are as welcome as the rich at his throne of grace.

Verse 3 — Find refuge before the storm

Faith sees the judgment approaching sinners and turns to Jesus Christ as the sure refuge.

Verse 4 — Reverence produces humility

The fear of the Lord leads to humility, spiritual riches and ultimately eternal life.

Verse 5 — Two very different paths

The way of sin is dangerous and distressing, while the way of duty is safe and good.

Verse 6 — Train children toward the Savior

Raise children not along the path their fallen hearts naturally choose, but in the way they should follow. Lead each child to know the Savior as early as possible.

Verse 7 — Beware unnecessary debts

The danger of debt makes it important to avoid careless borrowing and obligations. Though rich and poor differ in this life, remember that the Lord governs the difference.

Verse 8 — Misused power fails

The strength and authority abused by wicked people will not last.

Verse 9 — Compassion receives blessing

Those who seek to relieve other people's needs and suffering receive God's blessing.

Verse 10 — Scoffing destroys peace

Profane mockers and slanderers disturb peaceful fellowship.

Verse 11 — Sincerity and divine friendship

God becomes the Friend of those whose hearts are without deceit. This honor belongs to all his faithful people.

Verse 12 — The defeat of treachery

God turns the clever plans of dishonest and treacherous people toward their own confusion.

Verse 13 — Laziness invents a lion

The lazy person imagines a lion waiting outdoors while ignoring the real danger of the devil—the roaring lion—and of idleness destroying the soul.

Verse 14 — Sexual impurity clouds judgment

Sexual wrongdoing can so darken the mind that recovery becomes exceedingly difficult.

Verse 15 — Foolishness in the human heart

Sinful folly belongs to human nature from childhood and clings to the soul. We all need correction from our heavenly Father.

Verse 16 — Responsible stewardship

We are stewards of what God entrusts to us and must use his gifts according to his will.

Verses 17–21 — Listen and trust God's word

Bend the ear to God's teaching and apply the heart to it through faith and love. The foundation of practical religion is delighting in God and depending upon him. The sure way to understand the truth of God's word is to live conscientiously according to it.

Verses 22 and 23 — Defend the poor

Those who exploit and oppress poor people do so at great danger to themselves. If others refuse to defend them, God himself will take up their cause.

Verses 24 and 25 — Avoid contagious anger

Our fallen hearts contain so much dry tinder that close association with people continually throwing sparks of anger is dangerous.

Verses 26 and 27 — Do not waste what families need

Everyone owes justice to themselves and their families. Carelessly guaranteeing debts or wasting needed possessions violates that duty.

Verse 28 — Respect property and work diligently

Do not infringe on another person's rightful property. True diligence is rare and valuable: it can lift people to higher responsibility. Most importantly, be diligent in God's work and in the duties of faith.

modern_osis:
Verses 1–3 — Restrain appetite

God's limits upon our appetites are intended to protect us from injuring ourselves.

Verses 4 and 5 — Do not make wealth your goal

Do not become someone whose whole purpose is getting rich. Worldly possessions cannot satisfy the soul, and even what we grasp firmly cannot be held for long.

Verses 6–8 — Avoid insincere hospitality; welcome God's feast

Do not make yourself dependent upon people whose welcome is insincere. But when God invites us to his own feast, we can safely receive the Bread of Life and delight in his provision (Isaiah 25:6; 55:2).

Verse 9 — Know when silence is appropriate

We ought to speak about God's truth whenever there is a fitting opportunity, but when someone plainly refuses to listen, wisdom sometimes requires silence.

Verses 10 and 11 — God protects the fatherless

Fatherless children receive God's special care. He is their mighty Redeemer, fully able to defend them.

Verses 12–16 — Teach and lovingly correct children

A parent urges a child to give serious attention to Scripture, corrects wrongdoing with prayer while trusting God's blessing, and encourages obedience by showing what will bring genuine good. What joy parents have when children follow this faithful teaching!

Verses 17 and 18 — Do not envy temporary prosperity

The believer's hope will not be disappointed. Both present trials and the apparent prosperity of sinners are drawing toward their end.

Verses 19–28 — Give the whole heart to God

The gracious Savior purchased pardon and peace and calls us with a loving parent's affection to listen, become wise and follow his guidance. Young people should heed godly parents: when the heart is directed, the steps follow. Buy the truth and never sell it, not even for pleasure, honor or wealth. God requires the whole heart, not a portion divided between himself and the world. Follow Scripture, Providence and faithful examples. Guard particularly against drunkenness, which dulls the mind, and sexual immorality, which takes away the heart due to God and is difficult to escape once welcomed.

Verses 29–35 — The self-destruction of drunkenness

Avoid even the beginnings of alcohol's sinful allurements. Excess brings strife, impurity, insolence, uncontrolled speech and dulled conscience. A drunken person may face mortal danger yet feel secure, like someone sleeping atop a ship's mast. Even while judgment approaches, the person may insist, “I will seek it again.” What sensible person would sell themselves to a habit that risks dying senseless and waking under judgment? Henry understands Wisdom's words as Christ addressing sinners.

Verses 10-11

[Prov.23.12-Prov.23.16]
Verses 12-16
Here is a parent instructing his child to give his mind to the Scriptures. Here is a parent correcting his child: accompanied with prayer, and blessed of God, it may prove a means of preventing his destruction. Here is a parent encouraging his child, telling him what would be for his good. And what a comfort it would be, if herein he answered his expectation!
[Prov.23.17-Prov.23.18]
Verses 17-18
The believer's expectation shall not be disappointed; the end of his trials, and of the sinner's prosperity, is at hand.
[Prov.23.19-Prov.23.28]
Verses 19-28
The gracious Saviour who purchased pardon and peace for his people, with all the affection of a tender parent, counsels us to hear and be wise, and is ready to guide our hearts in his way. Here we have an earnest call to young people, to attend to the advice of their godly parents. If the heart be guided, the steps will be guided. Buy the truth, and sell it not; be willing to part with any thing for it. Do not part with it for pleasures, honours, riches, or any thing in this world. The heart is what the great God requires. We must not think to divide the heart between God and the world; he will have all or none. Look to the rule of God's word, the conduct of his providence, and the good examples of his people. Particular cautions are given against sins most destructive to wisdom and grace in the soul. It is really a shame to make a god of the belly. Drunkenness stupifies men, and then all goes to ruin. Licentiousness takes away the heart that should be given to God. Take heed of any approaches toward this sin, it is very hard to retreat from it. It bewitches men to their ruin.
[Prov.23.29-Prov.23.35]
Verses 29-35
Solomon warns against drunkenness. Those that would be kept from sin, must keep from all the beginnings of it, and fear coming within reach of its allurements. Foresee the punishment, what it will at last end in, if repentance prevent not. It makes men quarrel. Drunkards wilfully make woe and sorrow for themselves. It makes men impure and insolent. The tongue grows unruly; the heart utters things contrary to reason, religion, and common civility. It stupifies and besots men. They are in danger of death, of damnation; as much exposed as if they slept upon the top of a mast, yet feel secure. They fear no peril when the terrors of the Lord are before them; they feel no pain when the judgments of God are actually upon them. So lost is a drunkard to virtue and honour, so wretchedly is his conscience seared, that he is not ashamed to say, I will seek it again. With good reason we were bid to stop before the beginning. Who that has common sense would contract a habit, or sell himself to a sin, which tends to such guilt and misery, and exposes a man every day to the danger of dying insensible, and awaking in hell? Wisdom seems in these chapters to take up the discourse as at the beginning of the book. They must be considered as the words of Christ to the sinner.

modern_osis:
Verses 1 and 2 — Do not envy sinners

Never long to cast away God's restraints in order to live like those who reject him.

Verses 3–6 — Wisdom builds and strengthens

Godliness and prudence in outward affairs together form a wise person. Knowledge fills the soul with the Spirit's graces and comforts and strengthens us for spiritual service and warfare.

Verses 7–9 — Do not surrender to ignorance or devise harm

The foolish imagine wisdom is beyond them and refuse to seek it. Doing evil is wrong, but planning evil is worse. Even sinful thoughts as they first arise require repentance. People who try to make others hateful often become hateful themselves.

Verse 10 — Take heart in trouble

Trouble can tempt us to despair. Be courageous, and God will strengthen your heart.

Verses 11 and 12 — Rescue those in danger

If someone is threatened by an unjust action, we must do everything within our power to help. How much more should we seek to rescue immortal souls through our words and example?

Verses 13 and 14 — Taste the sweetness of wisdom

The pleasure and benefit of wisdom should move us to seek it. Most people readily enjoy sweet food, but too many have no taste for truth that is sweet to a renewed soul and makes us wise for salvation.

Verses 15 and 16 — The righteous rise after falling

Sincere believers may stumble like travelers over a stone, but they get up and proceed with greater care. Henry says this refers chiefly to falling into affliction rather than actual sin.

Verses 17 and 18 — Do not rejoice over an enemy's distress

We are forbidden to take sinful pleasure in the calamity of our enemies.

Verses 19 and 20 — Do not envy the prosperity of the wicked

Whatever outward success evildoers enjoy, it does not amount to true happiness.

Verses 21 and 22 — Faithfulness and social peace

Godly people promote peace in their communities. Better changes may sometimes be necessary, but avoid restless people who delight in upheaval.

Verses 23–26 — Be fair and give an honest answer

God's wisdom equips people for the duties of their positions. A fair and well-suited answer earns the lasting gratitude of those it benefits.

Verse 27 — Provide necessities before extras

Attend to necessary work and responsibilities before optional comforts. Do not go into debt carelessly.

Verses 28 and 29 — The duties of a truthful witness

Henry observes that these verses identify three faults of a witness. We should examine the warnings carefully and avoid giving false or retaliatory testimony.

Verses 30–34 — The neglected field and neglected soul

Farming is a blessing: without it the earth would be a wilderness. Even ordinary work is ruined by laziness and self-indulgence. Fields full of thorns and broken walls picture hearts left untended, where sinful desires grow as people fall asleep spiritually. Let that sight move us to greater diligence in every good work.

modern_osis:
Verses 1–3 — God knows all; rulers must investigate

God never needs to investigate: nothing can be hidden from him. Rulers, however, are honored when they carefully search out matters and bring hidden wrongdoing into the light.

Verses 4 and 5 — Reforming government

A ruler best establishes a government by removing evil and correcting vice among the people.

Verses 6 and 7 — Choose humility before honor

True religion teaches humility and self-denial. Anyone who has seen God's glory in Jesus Christ recognizes personal unworthiness.

Verses 8–10 — Prevent unnecessary disputes

Rushing into conflict produces needless difficulty. Every war eventually ends; often it would be better not to have begun. The same is true of private quarrels: do everything possible to settle them.

Verses 11 and 12 — Words that suit their moment

Counsel and correction offered at the proper time are beautiful, like fine fruit enhanced by a vessel of silver.

Verse 13 — Be a faithful messenger

The aim of anyone entrusted with a task is to carry it out faithfully. We should especially welcome a faithful minister who serves as Christ's messenger.

Verse 14 — Do not claim gifts you have not given

Those who pretend to possess or have given gifts they never had are like clouds promising rain but leaving the fields dry.

Verse 15 — Persuasion needs patience

Bear a temporary injury patiently and speak without anger. Gentle persuasion is often more effective than force against a stubborn mind.

Verse 16 — Good things require moderation

God permits us to enjoy pleasant things, but warns against excess.

Verse 17 — Be a considerate neighbor

Even sincere neighbors need discretion to live peacefully together. God is a better Friend than any human friend: the more often we come to him, the more welcome we are.

Verse 18 — False testimony injures

A lying witness brings danger into every matter in which testimony is needed.

Verse 19 — An unreliable helper increases pain

Trusting an unfaithful person during hardship brings not merely disappointment but additional suffering.

Verse 20 — Do not trivialize sorrow

Trying to comfort grieving people by forcing merriment upon them is the wrong approach.

Verses 21 and 22 — Love even enemies

Loving enemies is already commanded in the Old Testament. Jesus Christ provided the supreme example, loving us while we were his enemies.

Verse 23 — Do not reward slander with attention

Slander would be spoken less readily if people did not eagerly listen to it. Sin loses courage when it meets firm resistance.

Verse 24 — Choose peace over miserable companionship

Solitude is better than sharing life with someone who continually destroys its peace.

Verse 25 — Good news from the far country

Heaven is a distant homeland. How refreshing is its news in the everlasting gospel, and in the Spirit's witness that we are God's children!

Verse 26 — When the righteous yield to sin

A righteous person led into wrongdoing harms others like a public spring whose waters have become poisoned.

Verse 27 — Resist excessive appetite and praise

By grace we must learn to deny not only bodily indulgence but also craving for other people's admiration.

Verse 28 — Ask the Spirit for self-control

Verse 1 — Honor must be fitting

It is inappropriate to grant honor to people unfit or unworthy to receive it.

Verse 2 — A baseless curse cannot injure

A curse spoken without cause does no more lasting harm than a bird flying over someone's head.

Verse 3 — Correction suited to character

Every creature must be treated according to its nature. Careless and wicked people often refuse persuasion or reason. Human beings are naturally untamed, but God's grace changes some hearts.

Verses 4 and 5 — Answer fools with discernment

Choose how to respond according to the person and circumstances, addressing the conscience in whatever way may best end the dispute.

Verses 6–9 — Foolishness misuses wise sayings

Fools are unfit to carry important messages or receive great honors. Even wise proverbs lose their value when handled or applied foolishly.

Verse 10 — Two possible meanings of divine judgment

Henry allows two readings: the Creator will deal with sinners according to guilt, or powerful human rulers should disgrace and punish wicked conduct. Neither possibility should be silently replaced by the other.

Verse 11 — Returning to sin

A dog returning to its own filth is a revolting image of sinners who repeatedly return to their vices (2 Peter 2:22).

Verse 12 — The danger of self-conceit

Some people know very little yet are extraordinarily proud of it. They resemble those who think their spiritual condition is sound when it is desperately wrong.

Verse 13 — Imaginary dangers and real duties

The lazy person fears work and invents dangers. It is foolish to avoid a real duty through imagined difficulties, especially duties of faith.

Verse 14 — Movement without progress

Love of bodily ease produces spiritual sickness. Some religious people resemble a door turning on its hinges: they perform outward exercises but make no progress toward heaven because the world and flesh hold them fast.

Verse 15 — Laziness refuses even nourishment

The idle person may leave bed but still accomplish nothing. People neglecting duty often claim they cannot perform it. The spiritually lazy refuse to feed their souls on the Bread of Life or draw near in prayer for promised blessings.

Verse 16 — Labor in the Lord is not wasted

People who work diligently in spiritual service know they serve a good Master, and their labor will not be in vain.

Verse 17 — Avoid meddling in others' quarrels

Interfering without necessity in other people's disputes is a way of deliberately exposing ourselves to temptation.

Verses 18 and 19 — Do not excuse harm as a joke

People who sin as a joke must repent seriously or their wrongdoing will destroy them.

Verses 20–22 — Gossip sustains quarrels

Conflict can inflame families and communities. Whispering and malicious backbiting often kindle and feed the fire.

Verse 23 — The disguise of an evil heart

A wicked heart covered by attractive speech resembles a broken piece of pottery coated with the waste of silver.

Verses 24–26 — Beware flattering deceit

Be cautious of pleasing words unless the speaker's character is trustworthy. Satan spoke attractively to Eve; trusting his flattering temptations was ruinous.

Verse 27 — Schemes rebound upon their makers

Plotting evil is hard work, like digging a pit or rolling a heavy stone, but the plotter is often preparing the danger for himself.

Verse 28 — Two kinds of destructive lies

Henry distinguishes slandering lies, whose harm is plain, from flattering lies, which destroy secretly. A wise person may have more reason to fear a flatterer than a slanderer.

Verse 1 — Do not presume on tomorrow

We do not know what tomorrow may bring. This does not forbid sensible preparation; it forbids assuming tomorrow is guaranteed. Do not postpone the one necessary work of conversion.

Verse 2 — Avoid praising yourself

There may be times to defend your conduct, but self-praise is not fitting.

Verses 3 and 4 — Uncontrolled passion is a heavy burden

People unable to govern their emotions are often crushed by the weight of those passions.

Verses 5 and 6 — Faithful correction is love

A plain and sincere rebuke is better than hidden hatred or affection that praises a person while allowing sin to destroy the soul.

Verse 7 — Hunger makes the gospel sweet

Poor people often appreciate their modest comforts more and thank God for them more sincerely. Likewise the self-satisfied disdain the gospel, while those hungry for righteousness receive comfort even from a simple book or sermon about Christ.

Verse 8 — A proper place for duty

People have their own responsibilities and places in society where they can serve safely and contentedly.

Verses 9 and 10 — The nearer and better Friend

Do not assume relatives can help merely because of kinship. Seek trustworthy help from those able to respond. Above all there is a Friend closer than a brother; place complete confidence in him.

Verse 11 — Good conduct honors the gospel

Wise parents desire children whose prudent lives bring them joy. Likewise believers' consistent behavior offers the strongest answer to people who criticize the gospel.

Verse 12 — Do not walk toward temptation

People who knowingly expose themselves to temptation may fall into sin and reap painful consequences.

Verse 13 — Do not ruin yourself with rash debts

Someone may become poor while remaining honest. But it is not honest to bring ruin upon oneself through reckless financial undertakings.

Verse 14 — Beware craving praise

Loving admiration for its own sake is foolish and exposes us to the temptation of pride.

Verses 15 and 16 — Relentless quarreling

A neighbor's quarrel may be like a brief, sharp shower; perpetual disputes within marriage resemble continuous rain.

Verse 17 — Make one another wiser

Be thoughtful about whom you keep company with. Let the aim of conversation be to help one another grow wiser and better.

Verse 18 — Faithful service receives honor

Even a tiring or socially despised occupation can bring worthwhile results when performed faithfully. God honors those who serve him loyally.

Verse 19 — Examine the heart

Corrupt hearts resemble one another, as do hearts sanctified by God: the first bear the earthly image, the second the heavenly. Compare your own heart carefully with Scripture.

Verse 20 — Unsatisfied sin; satisfied faith

Death and sinful desire are never satisfied. The worldly heart always wants more profit or pleasure. Those looking toward the Lord, however, find their satisfaction in him forever.

Verse 21 — Praise tests character

As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, a person's character is tested by the way praise is received.

Verse 22 — Grace alone renews entrenched sin

Some people remain hardened even under severe correction. Only God's recreating grace can finally change a heart.

Verses 23–27 — Diligence, Providence and lasting treasure

Everyone should pursue useful work rather than idleness or interfering in matters they do not understand. Work diligently and wisely. Yet nothing earthly can be permanently secured, so choose a lasting inheritance. Trust God's blessing upon honest labor to provide as much temporal prosperity as is genuinely good for us.

Verse 1 — Sin makes cowards

Sinful people are often fearful. Those walking in their duty before God can remain courageous even amid real difficulties.

Verse 2 — Public wrongdoing disturbs a nation

A nation's sins undermine its public peace and stability.

Verse 3 — Oppression by the needy

When poor or needy people obtain power to exploit others, they may oppress more severely than the already wealthy.

Verse 4 — Sin encourages sin

Wicked people support and strengthen one another in their wrongdoing.

Verse 5 — Seek God to understand rightly

Seeking the Lord is evidence of some true understanding and one of the best means of gaining more.

Verse 6 — Godly poverty is better

An honest and reverent poor person is better than a wealthy but ungodly one, having greater inward comfort and bringing more good to the world.

Verse 7 — Bad company shames a family

Those who join the company of reckless people both grieve their parents and bring shame on them.

Verse 8 — Dishonest gain cannot endure

Wealth acquired through evil practices will not last, however large it grows. God may use its loss to help the poor and honor his justice.

Verse 9 — Do not reject God's commands while praying

The prayer that displeases God comes from someone who stubbornly refuses obedience to his known word.

Verse 10 — The misery of wicked success

The apparent success of ungodly people ultimately contributes to their own suffering.

Verse 11 — Wealth can blind judgment

Rich people are often flattered until they imagine themselves superior to everyone else.

Verse 12 — Freedom for the righteous benefits the land

A nation enjoys honor and well-being when faithful people have liberty.

Verse 13 — Confess sin to receive mercy

Excusing and concealing sin cannot bring real peace. Whoever confesses sin humbly with genuine repentance and faith finds mercy. The Son of God is our great atoning sacrifice; in our guilt and danger we may seek the mercy that reigns through righteousness to eternal life in Jesus Christ.

Verse 14 — Reverent fear without terror

There is a holy fear that brings happiness. Faith and love deliver believers from the fear of eternal condemnation, but we should always fear offending God and falling into sin.

Verse 15 — A wicked ruler is a predator

Whatever title society gives a cruel ruler, Scripture compares that ruler to a roaring lion and a roaming bear.

Verse 16 — Oppression is foolish

Oppressors lack understanding and damage even their own honor, ease and security.

Verse 17 — The burden of murder

People guilty of murder may be pursued by overwhelming terror. Henry speaks of their deserved punishment and the reluctance of others to protect them from it.

Verse 18 — Uprightness brings security

Integrity gives people holy confidence even in dangerous times, while dishonest and deceitful people can never feel truly secure.

Verse 19 — Honest labor provides

Diligent people choose the path toward a stable and comfortable livelihood.

Verse 20 — Holiness and honesty before quick wealth

The best route to happiness is a holy, honest life, not gaining a fortune rapidly without regard for right or wrong.

Verse 21 — Judgment must be impartial

Justice is corrupted whenever any consideration other than what is truly right governs a decision.

Verse 22 — Riches can vanish

People who rush to become wealthy seldom reflect on how quickly God may strip them of riches and leave them poor.

Verse 23 — Faithful rebuke is better than flattery

After reflection, most people value someone who corrected them honestly more than someone who merely soothed them with praise.

Verse 24 — Do not exploit parents

It is wicked to treat robbing one's parents as no sin, whether through manipulation, threats, squandering their goods or running up debts against them.

Verse 25 — Trusting grace brings peace

Those who continually depend upon God and his grace, living by faith, find inward rest.

Verse 26 — Do not trust the deceitful heart

A fool places confidence in personal strength, merit and righteousness, and in a heart that is deceitful and has already misled that person many times.

Verse 27 — Look for people in need

A selfish person not only fails to seek opportunities for compassion, but deliberately looks away when the need becomes visible.

Verse 28 — Wicked authority and Christ in Proverbs

When power belongs to the wicked, wise people may withdraw from public office. Henry concludes that even where Proverbs seem to speak least directly of Christ, careful reading will uncover truths that lead to him.

Verse 1 — Flee from the coming judgment

If God wounds, who can heal? His word warns everyone to flee from the wrath to come and take hold of the hope set before us in Jesus Christ.

Verse 2 — Righteousness in government

People have reason to rejoice when their rulers are righteous and to mourn when those rulers are wicked.

Verse 3 — Wisdom protects against lust

Verse 4 — Christ rules with justice

The Lord Jesus is the King who will administer true justice among his people.

Verse 5 — Flattery disarms

Flatterers cause people to lower their guard, making it easier to draw them into foolish behavior.

Verse 6 — Sin entangles; righteousness frees

Transgression ends in distress, while righteous people walk in liberty and safety.

Verse 7 — Care for the poor

The righteous show compassion for people in poverty and distress. The wicked disregard their needs without feeling.

Verse 8 — Mockery and public peace

Scornful people laugh at holy and serious matters. Those who advance true religion and wisdom help turn away God's wrath.

Verse 9 — Argument with a conceited person

When a wise person disputes with a quarrelsome, conceited opponent, anger or ridicule often follows, and little good results.

Verse 10 — Love for those who hate us

Christ warned his disciples that people would hate them. Yet the righteous, even when hated by bloodthirsty people, willingly do what they can for those people's salvation.

Verse 11 — Keep counsel

A fool says everything that comes to mind or has been learned and cannot keep a confidence.

Verse 12 — Bad leadership spreads lies

A ruler who welcomes flatterers and listens to slander makes liars and false accusers of those who serve him.

Verse 13 — All live under God's gifts

Some people are poor, while others possess great wealth dishonestly acquired. They meet in daily business, and God supplies life's comforts to both. He also gives saving grace to some among both groups.

Verse 14 — Defend those without power

Rich people usually look after their own interests. A ruler should protect poor and needy people and plead their cause.

Verse 15 — Correct children wisely

Parents should consider both the good that comes from appropriate correction and the harm caused by excessive indulgence.

Verse 16 — Do not be shaken by growing evil

Believers should not allow the multiplication of wickedness and wicked people to overthrow their faith or hope. Wait patiently upon the Lord.

Verse 17 — Do not neglect necessary correction

When children act wrongly, parents must not simply leave them without correction.

Verse 18 — The precious open vision of Christ

A place without Bibles and faithful ministers is spiritually exposed and vulnerable to the enemy of souls. The gospel is an open vision revealing Christ: it humbles sinners, exalts the Savior and promotes holiness in everyday conduct. These precious truths sustain spiritual life and preserve souls from destruction.

Verse 19 — Serving only from fear

The servant described here is lazy, unprofitable and wicked. The service arises neither from love nor from conscience, but only from fear.

Verse 20 — Rash self-conceit

A self-important person who speaks rashly and constantly quarrels can be less open to correction than even ignorant or openly immoral people.

Verse 21 — Kindness is not indulgence

Good treatment of a servant does not mean indulgence that ultimately ruins the servant, just as it could ruin a child. The body serves the soul: pampering its every demand encourages it to forget that proper relationship.

Verse 22 — The fruit of an angry spirit

A passionate, angry disposition provokes other people and also offends God.

Verse 23 — Humility before honor

Only those who humble themselves will be exalted and firmly established.

Verse 24 — Receiving stolen goods

Someone knowingly receiving stolen property shares in the thief's wrongdoing.

Verse 25 — Do not be ashamed of Christ

Many people are ashamed to acknowledge Christ now. He will not acknowledge them at judgment. But trust in the Lord saves us from this snare.

Verse 26 — Seek the supreme Ruler's favor

The wisest course is to seek God's favor, for he is the Ruler of rulers. Every creature becomes to us what God makes that creature to be.

Verse 27 — Hate sin, not souls

The righteous hate the wicked person's sin and avoid corrupting company. Christ exposed human wickedness but prayed for his persecutors while they crucified him. A Christian must hate sin within oneself and others, while seeking sinners' salvation. Those who remain unholy, however, have a deep hostility to godliness.

Verses 1–6 — Agur's humility and God's sufficient word

Agur describes himself as lacking righteousness and having acted foolishly. We should likewise think humbly about ourselves.

He says he needs revelation to guide him into truth and wisdom. The more understanding people gain, the more clearly they see how much they do not know. They become eager to discover still more of God and the riches of his grace in Jesus Christ.

Henry understands verse 4 as a prophetic reference to the One who descended from heaven to become our Teacher and Savior, then ascended to heaven as our Advocate.

The Messiah is presented here, in Henry's reading, as a Person distinct from the Father, although his name remained hidden at that time.

Even the Redeemer's wonderful works of providence and grace cannot be completely searched out. Without Christ, Henry says, the foundations of the earth would have sunk beneath the curse brought upon creation through human sin.

Who is the mighty One accomplishing all this?

God's word lacks nothing necessary to fulfill its purpose. Adding to it opens the way for error and corruption.

Verses 7–9 — Neither poverty nor riches

Agur wisely asks to be kept in a middle condition, away from the temptations associated with both poverty and wealth.

He prays for daily bread appropriate to his circumstances, family and genuine welfare. His prayer strikingly resembles parts of the Lord's Prayer.

If God removes vanity and lies from us, grants us a share in Christ's pardoning love, becomes our portion and teaches us to walk with him, we have far more than everything we need spiritually.

People who possess abundance are tempted to abuse it. Poverty also brings distress and temptation.

That is why Agur's prayer is wise, although seldom offered sincerely.

What is appropriate provision for one person or family may not be appropriate for another. We can nevertheless trust our heavenly Father to provide whatever is genuinely good for us.

Why should we desire more than that?

Verse 10 — Do not slander a servant

Do not maliciously accuse a servant to an employer, even in relatively small matters, in order to cause trouble.

Verses 11–14 — Four kinds of deeply corrupt people

Every age contains people who repay their parents' care with monstrous ingratitude.

Others persuade themselves they are holy while secretly practicing wickedness and cherishing sinful hearts.

Still others display outrageous pride.

And in every age there have been people of exceptional cruelty.

Verses 15–17 — Greed, cruelty and contempt for parents

Cruelty and covetousness are like the two daughters of the leech, endlessly demanding, “Give, give!”

Such passions never give their owners peace. They resemble four things that can never be satisfied.

People who continually crave more wealth are never truly rich.

Many who came to a terrible end later acknowledged that their wicked course began when they despised their parents' authority.

Verses 18–20 — Wonders of nature and the hidden ways of sin

Four things lie beyond complete human understanding.

Nature itself is full of astonishing mysteries.

But Henry describes the fourth example as a mystery of iniquity: the tactics through which a corrupt seducer wins a woman's affection and those through which an immoral woman conceals her misconduct.

His comments here concern the hidden tactics of wrongdoing, not a claim that every relationship or woman resembles these examples.

Verses 21–23 — Four kinds of troublesome people

Henry describes four types of people whose behavior causes considerable disturbance.

The first is someone who rises from humble beginnings to authority but possesses a base and tyrannical spirit. The problem is not poverty or low birth, but the abuse of power.

The second is a foolish, violent person given over to excess.

The third is a woman with a contentious spirit and corrupt habits.

The fourth is a servant who gains improper influence and abuses it.

Those whom Providence raises from humble circumstances should particularly guard against temptations that could corrupt their new position.

Verses 24–28 — Wisdom learned from small creatures

Four small creatures deserve our admiration for their wisdom.

They remind us that people who are poor, obscure and considered of little importance in the present world may nevertheless be wise concerning their own souls and the life to come.

Verses 29–33 — Self-government and peace

We can learn appropriate conduct even from animals.

We should learn particularly to govern our temper when others provoke us.

An evil thought must not be allowed to become evil speech. Nor should we stir up anger in other people.

Let us act and speak without violence, showing gentleness and calmness.

How often we have acted foolishly in rebellion against the Lord our King!

Let us humble ourselves before him.

Having found peace with God, let us pursue peace with everyone.

[Prov.30.1-Prov.30.6]
Chapter 30
Verses 1-6
Agur speaks of himself as wanting a righteousness, and having done very foolishly. And it becomes us all to have low thoughts of ourselves. He speaks of himself as wanting revelation to guide him in the ways of truth and wisdom. The more enlightened people are, the more they lament their ignorance; the more they pray for clearer, still clearer discoveries of God, and his rich grace in Christ Jesus. In ver.#(4), there is a prophetic notice of Him who came down from heaven to be our Instructor and Saviour, and then ascended into heaven to be our Advocate. The Messiah is here spoken of as a Person distinct from the Father, but his name as yet secret. The great Redeemer, in the glories of his providence and grace, cannot be found out to perfection. Had it not been for Christ, the foundations of the earth had sunk under the load of the curse upon the ground, for man's sin. Who, and what is the mighty One that doeth all this? There is not the least ground to suspect anything wanting in the word of God; adding to his words opens the way to errors and corruptions.
[Prov.30.7-Prov.30.9]
Verses 7-9
Agur wisely prayed for a middle state, that he might be kept at a distance from temptations; he asked daily bread suited to his station, his family, and his real good. There is a remarkable similarity between this prayer and several clauses of the Lord's prayer. If we are removed from vanity and lies; if we are interested in the pardoning love of Christ, and have him for our portion; if we walk with God, then we shall have all we can ask or think, as to spiritual things. When we consider how those who have abundance are prone to abuse the gift, and what it is to suffer want, Agur's prayer will ever be found a wise one, though seldom offered. Food convenient; what is so for one, may not be so for another; but we may be sure that our heavenly Father will supply all our need, and not suffer us to want anything good for us; and why should we wish for more?
[Prov.30.10]
Verse 10
Slander not a servant to his master, accuse him not in small matters, to make mischief.
[Prov.30.11-Prov.30.14]
Verses 11-14
In every age there are monsters of ingratitude who ill-treat their parents. Many persuade themselves they are holy persons, whose hearts are full of sin, and who practise secret wickedness. There are others whose lofty pride is manifest. There have also been cruel monsters in every age.
[Prov.30.15-Prov.30.17]
Verses 15-17
Cruelty and covetousness are two daughters of the horseleech, that still cry, "Give, give," and they are continually uneasy to themselves. Four things never are satisfied, to which these devourers are compared. Those are never rich that are always coveting. And many who have come to a bad end, have owned that their wicked courses began by despising their parents' authority.
[Prov.30.18-Prov.30.20]
Verses 18-20
Four things cannot be fully known. The kingdom of nature is full of marvels. The fourth is a mystery of iniquity; the cursed arts by which a vile seducer gains the affections of a female; and the arts which a vile woman uses to conceal her wickedness.
[Prov.30.21-Prov.30.23]
Verses 21-23
Four sorts of persons are very troublesome. Men of low origin and base spirit, who, getting authority, become tyrants. Foolish and violent men indulging in excesses. A woman of a contentious spirit and vicious habits. A servant who has obtained undue influence. Let those whom Providence has advanced from low beginnings, carefully watch against that sin which most easily besets them.
[Prov.30.24-Prov.30.28]
Verses 24-28
Four things that are little, are yet to be admired. There are those who are poor in the world, and of small account, yet wise for their souls and another world.
[Prov.30.29-Prov.30.33]
Verses 29-33
We may learn from animals to go well; also to keep our temper under all provocations. We must keep the evil thought in our minds from breaking out into evil speeches. We must not stir up the passions of others. Let nothing be said or done with violence, but every thing with softness and calmness. Alas, how often have we done foolishly in rising up against the Lord our King! Let us humble ourselves before him. And having found peace with Him, let us follow peace with all men.
